summary: Describes the Telnet server interface on IBM's iSeries midrange computers, which lets clients request terminal or printer sessions with specific attributes such as device names, encryption, language support and auto-sign-on. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4777 describes what an IBM iSeries Telnet server accepts from a client. The client can send extra named settings inside the Telnet environment option, such as the name of the device it wants and the keyboard layout and character set it needs, and it can send its password encrypted or as a Kerberos ticket. The server answers with a record saying which device it gave and whether the sign-on worked.

questions: how does iseries telnet auto sign on
subtitle: How a Telnet client asks an IBM iSeries server for a particular terminal or printer session, and signs on automatically.

tldr.problem: A Telnet client could ask for a kind of terminal but not for a particular named device, could not set the device's attributes, and had to sign on a second time at the server's own sign-on panel.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines new USERVAR variables carried in the Telnet environment option of RFC 1572, covering device names and attributes, an encrypted or Kerberos sign-on, and the startup response record that tells the client what the server actually did.
tldr.outcome: The client can now name the device it wants, ask for the code page, character set and keyboard type it wants, bypass the sign-on panel when the server's QRMTSIGN setting allows it, and read the outcome from a response record. It is an Informational document.

today: RFC 4777 is an Informational memo published in November 2006, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It revises RFC 2877, and its support functions are built on the Telnet environment option negotiation of RFC 1572.

sections.title: What the iSeries Telnet Server Adds
sections.content:
The iSeries Telnet server enables clients to negotiate both terminal and printer device names through Telnet environment option negotiation. This allows Telnet servers and clients to exchange environment information using a set of standard or custom variables. By using a combination of both standard VARs and custom USERVARs, the iSeries Telnet server allows a client to request a pre-defined specific device by name.

If no pre-defined device exists, then the device will be created, with the client having the option to negotiate device attributes such as the code page, character set and keyboard type. Since printers can now be negotiated as a device name, new terminal types have been defined to request printers, so that IBM-3812-1 and IBM-5553-B01 can now be negotiated as valid TERMINAL-TYPE options.

The server also allows the exchange of user profile and password information, where the password may be in either plain text or encrypted form. If a valid combination of profile and password is received, then the client is allowed to bypass the sign-on panel. The local server setting of the QRMTSIGN system value must be either *VERIFY or *SAMEPRF for the bypass of the sign-on panel to succeed. These support functions are implemented primarily using the Telnet environment option negotiation of RFC 1572, which defines new USERVAR variables that the iSeries Telnet server recognises.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a Telnet client tells the server what kind of screen it wants, and the server makes one. This memo describes how the client can also name a particular device, ask for particular settings, and sign in without typing a password at a second prompt.

sections.title: Enhanced Option Negotiation
sections.content:
Standard Telnet option negotiation typically begins with the server issuing an invitation to engage in terminal type negotiation, and the client and server then enter a series of sub-negotiations to determine the level of terminal support that will be used. After the terminal type is agreed, they normally negotiate a required set of additional options, such as EOR, BINARY and SGA, that are needed to support transparent mode or full screen 5250/3270 block mode support. As soon as the required options have been negotiated, the server suspends further negotiations and begins initializing the actual virtual device on the iSeries.

To accommodate the new environment option negotiations, the server bundles an environment option invitation along with the standard terminal type invitation. A client should either send a negative acknowledgment, WONT NEW-ENVIRON, or, at some point after completing terminal-type negotiations but before completing the full set of negotiations required for 5250 transparent mode, engage in environment option sub-negotiation with the server. A maximum of 1024 bytes of environment strings may be sent to the server.

The order matters. With an iSeries Telnet server several virtual device modes can be negotiated: a VTxxx device, a 3270 device, and a 5250 device, which includes Network Station. The mode selected depends on the terminal type negotiated plus any other Telnet option negotiations necessary to support it, and the server creates the virtual device at the first opportunity it thinks it has all the requested attributes. For transparent mode the moment TERMINAL-TYPE, BINARY and EOR are negotiated the server creates the device, so any NEW-ENVIRON negotiations received after that point have no effect on device attributes. For other device modes the client cannot be sure when the server will create the device, and it is in the client's best interest to send NEW-ENVIRON negotiations as soon as possible, preferably before TERMINAL-TYPE is negotiated, so that the requested attributes are received before the virtual device is created.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks for the environment variables early, and the client should send them before the terminal type is agreed, because the server builds the session as soon as it has the settings it needs.

sections.title: The USERVARs for Device Attributes
sections.content:
Telnet environment option USERVARs have been defined to allow a compliant Telnet client more control over the virtual device on the iSeries and to provide information to the server about the client. These USERVARs allow the client to create or select a previously created virtual device: if the virtual device does not exist and must be created, the USERVAR variables are used to create and initialize the device attributes, and if it already exists its attributes are modified.

Six USERVARs are defined for this purpose. DEVNAME carries the display device name, up to 10 characters. KBDTYPE carries the keyboard type, up to 3 characters. CODEPAGE carries the code page, up to 5 characters, and CHARSET the character set, up to 5 characters. IBMSENDCONFREC, set to YES or NO, says whether a startup response record is wanted. IBMASSOCPRT carries the name of a printer to associate with the display device, and that printer must currently exist on the server system.

CODEPAGE and CHARSET must be associated with a KBDTYPE. If either is sent without KBDTYPE they default to system values, and a default value for KBDTYPE can be sent to force the CODEPAGE and CHARSET values to be used. iSeries system objects such as device names, user profiles and plain text passwords are required to be specified in English uppercase, so uppercase ASCII values are recommended, and the server converts them to EBCDIC.
sections.plainLanguage: These named settings let the client say which device it wants and how that device should behave, such as which keyboard layout and character set to use.

sections.title: Auto-Sign-On and Password Encryption
sections.content:
To allow password encryption, two new USERVARs are used to exchange seed and substitute password information. IBMRSEED carries a random seed to be used in both the Data Encryption Standard and Secure Hash Algorithm password encryption, and IBMSUBSPW carries the encrypted copy of the password. The DES encryption uses the same 7-step DES-based password substitution scheme as APPC and Client Access, and the SHA encryption is the one described in FIPS 180-1. If encrypted password exchange is not required, plain text password exchange is permitted using the same USERVARs, with the random client seed set either to an empty value, the preferred method, or to hexadecimal zeros to indicate that the password is not encrypted.

To communicate the server random seed, the server requests a USERVAR name made up of the fixed part IBMRSEED immediately followed by an 8-byte hexadecimal server seed. The client generates its own 8-byte random seed value, uses both seeds to encrypt the password, and sends the encrypted password and the client seed to the server for authentication. Because these are variable length hexadecimal fields, the client must escape or byte stuff any bytes that could be seen as a Telnet environment option, specifically VAR, VALUE, ESC and USERVAR.

Auto-sign-on can also use a Kerberos ticket. The USERVAR IBMTICKET contains the complete Generic Security Services token, up to 16384 bytes, which the client obtains from a Key Distribution Center. Three further USERVARs give an auto-sign-on user more control over the startup environment: IBMCURLIB for the current library, IBMIMENU for the initial menu and IBMPROGRAM for the program to call, each up to 10 characters. If IBMSENDCONFREC is set to YES along with the automatic sign-on USERVARs, the client receives a startup response record containing a response code that says whether the automatic sign-on attempt succeeded.
sections.plainLanguage: The client can send its password encrypted, using a random number from the server and one of its own, or send a Kerberos ticket instead. Plain text passwords are allowed but the memo warns against them.

sections.title: Name Collisions and the Response Record
sections.content:
A device name collision occurs when a client sends the server a virtual device name that it wants to use, but that device is already in use on the server. When this occurs, the server sends a request to the client asking it to try another device name, using the USERVAR name DEVNAME to communicate it. The client sends all its environment variables including DEVNAME, and the server tries to select that device. If the device is already in use, the server asks for DEVNAME again as a single-variable request, and the client calculates a new value. If the new value is different from the last request the server tries it, otherwise the server disconnects the client. The server keeps asking until it receives a device that is not in use, or the same device name twice in a row.

The startup response record is how the server tells the client what actually happened. The IBMSENDCONFREC USERVAR asks the server to send it, and it contains the name of the display device that was actually acquired, a reason code if the attempt was unsuccessful, and the name of the Telnet server system. Among the success codes, I902 means the session was successfully started, and I906 means automatic sign-on was requested but is not allowed, with the session still allowed and a sign-on screen still to come. The error codes include 2702 device description not found, 2777 damaged device description, 8901 device not varied on, 8903 device not valid for session, 8916 no matching device found, 8936 security failure on session attempt and 8937 automatic sign-on rejected. For automatic sign-on without a Kerberos token there is a further set: 0001 system error, 0002 userid unknown, 0003 userid disabled, 0004 invalid password, passphrase or token, 0005 password, passphrase or token is expired, and 0008 a warning that the next invalid password or token will revoke the userid.
sections.plainLanguage: If the device the client asked for is already in use, the server asks for another name and keeps asking until it gets one that is free. The response record is then the server's report of what it did, including a code that says why anything went wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo points out that although passwords can now be encrypted using the IBMRSEED and IBMSUBSPW USERVAR negotiations, only the login passwords are encrypted and not the entire Telnet session. Encryption of the Telnet session requires that another protocol layer, such as SSL, be added. The auto-sign-on feature supports plain text passwords, encrypted passwords and Kerberos tokens, but using plain text passwords is strongly discouraged, and iSeries system administrators may want to configure their systems to reject plain text passwords.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting the password does not encrypt the rest of the session, so the data you type afterwards is still in the clear unless you add another layer such as SSL.

messages.label: IAC DO NEW-ENVIRON, IAC DO TERMINAL-TYPE
messages.note: The two requests are bundled together.

messages.label: IAC SB NEW-ENVIRON SEND
messages.note: The server asks for the environment variables, ending with IAC SE.

messages.label: IAC SB NEW-ENVIRON IS
messages.note: For example VAR USER VALUE JONES and USERVAR DEVNAME VALUE MYDEVICE07.

messages.label: IAC DO EOR
messages.note: The server then continues with the transparent mode options.

items.title: DEVNAME
items.text: Display device name, up to 10 characters.

items.text: YES or NO, asking for the startup response record.

items.title: IBMASSOCPRT
items.text: The printer associated with the display device.

items.label: SIGN-ON NOT ALLOWED
items.desc: Automatic sign-on requested, but not allowed. Session still allowed.

items.label: EXPIRED
items.desc: Password, passphrase or token is expired.
